# The Last Watch of the Mara Celeste

I brought her tea that morning. Black, no sugar, brewed past the point most people would drink it because Captain Wen had told me once, in the flat way she told you anything, that if she could see through it she didn't want it. I remember climbing the companionway with the mug in my right hand and my left braced against the wall, and that the angle of the climb felt wrong—steeper on the port side than it should have been, as though the stairs themselves had shifted in the night. They hadn't, of course. The ship had.

Wen was at the helm. I don't know how long she'd been there. Her hands were on the wheel and her eyes were somewhere past the glass, fixed on a distance I couldn't see because there was no distance—only a grey moving wall that was water and sky at once, undifferentiated, the whole world reduced to a single wet color. She wore the canvas jacket she always wore, the one with the ink stain on the left cuff from a pen she'd broken in March. Her hair was tied back. She looked, in that moment, exactly as she looked any other morning, and I think that was the first thing that frightened me.

I set the tea on the chart ledge, in the spot where the wood was already ring-stained from a hundred other mugs. She nodded. She didn't pick it up.

I went back down to the galley.

When I came up again—four hours later, maybe five, I had stopped trusting the clock on the galley wall because its ticking had become inaudible under the sound of the sea—the mug was still there. Full. A skin had formed on its surface, dark and faintly iridescent, the way cooling tea will do when it sits too long. The liquid was tilted at an angle that had nothing to do with the mug and everything to do with the ship. Wen was still at the wheel. Her hands had not moved. I took the mug back down and poured it out, and the tea ran sideways across the basin before it reached the drain.

That was the first day.

---

By evening the mate, whose name was Galvez, had the crew in the life raft. There were nine of them. I know because I counted the ration packs I carried up from the dry stores—nine meals times three days, twenty-seven foil packets in a canvas bag that I'd sealed with a double knot. I also packed the medical kit and six liters of fresh water and a bag of dried apricots I'd been saving for a cake I was never going to bake. Galvez checked the flares. The radio had been useless since noon.

I climbed to the wheelhouse to tell Wen.

She said no.

Not dramatically. Not through clenched teeth or with her jaw set in the way you imagine a captain's jaw when you hear this kind of story afterward, in a bar, from someone who wasn't there. She said it the way she'd say no to a second helping at dinner. Flat. Already past it.

I told her the raft was ready. She said she heard me. I told her Galvez was waiting. She said Galvez should go. I said the hull was taking water in the forward compartment and the bilge pumps were running at capacity and did she understand what that meant, and of course she did, she understood it better than I did, and I felt foolish for saying it, the way you feel foolish explaining to a doctor that their patient is bleeding.

"The men in Bermuda," she said.

I didn't understand.

"Burke and Lau. The assessors. And the bank's man, I forget his name, the one with the lisp. They have a registered lien, number—" She said a number. She said it precisely, the way you say a phone number you've dialed too many times. "If I bring her in, they take her. They've had the papers since October. It's all filed. It's done."

"If you don't bring her in," I said.

"Then she's my grandfather's boat."

She said it like that. Not *my grandfather's legacy*. Not *my grandfather's dream*. My grandfather's boat. The possessive of a woman referring to something attached to her body, something she wouldn't think to explain any more than she'd explain her own knuckles.

"You're staying," I said.

"Go with Galvez."

"You're staying to—what? Sink her?"

"I'm staying."

The typhoon said something enormous against the hull, and the wheelhouse windows went white with spray, and when they cleared Wen was still looking at me with an expression I could not then and cannot now accurately name. I thought, in the moment, that she was being brave. That's the first thing you think, isn't it? The captain who won't leave her ship. You reach for the noble version because the noble version is easy to hold.

But that isn't what I saw. What I saw was a woman who had memorized a lien number. Who spoke about repossession the way other people speak about amputation. Who would rather go to the bottom of the Pacific than watch a man with a lisp staple a notice to the wheelhouse door.

Spite, I thought. Or pride. Or grief dressed as stubbornness—some feeling she'd worn so long it had stiffened into something she could stand up in, like a coat left out in the frost.

I still don't know which.

I told Galvez to go.

---

During a lull—not calm, never calm, but a slackening, a half-breath between the waves—I went below to the galley and tried to heat soup on the stove. The stove had come loose from its gimbal mounts, so I wedged it into place with the two largest cutting boards and a folded towel, and I lit the burner, and I stood with my hand on the pot to keep it from sliding while the broth warmed. It was tinned minestrone, nothing I'd made myself. I'd stopped cooking actual meals around noon. There was no one to feed except Wen and she wasn't eating and the audience for my cooking had launched itself into the Pacific on a rubber raft four hours ago.

I had been on the *Mara Celeste* for fourteen months.

In that time I had learned her history the way you learn anything at sea—in pieces, sideways, without anyone ever sitting you down and explaining. The grandfather was named Wen Jia-hao and he had bought the ship in 1971 from a Panamanian outfit that was liquidating its coastal fleet. Or he had won her in a card game in Kaohsiung. Or he had built her himself in a yard in Keelung with borrowed money and lumber he'd salvaged from a dismantled church. There were at least three versions and Wen told none of them consistently and I think this was because the true version no longer mattered—what mattered was that there had always been a version, told at family tables, polished by retelling, the origin story of a household that happened to float.

Wen had grown up aboard. I knew this because of the door.

The door to the captain's cabin—Wen's cabin, and before that her father's cabin, and before that her grandfather's—had a series of pencil marks along its inside edge. Small horizontal lines with initials and dates. They started at knee height, which meant they started with a child. *J.W., 1982*. Then *J.W., 1983*. The initials changed as the decades passed—children and grandchildren pressed against the old wood, the pencil moving higher each year, the record of a family measuring itself against its own vessel. The most recent marks were from the 1990s. After that, the measuring had stopped, or the children had grown, or both.

I saw those marks every time I brought Wen her morning coffee. The cabin door was usually open. The marks were at eye level—the later ones—and I could read the dates without trying. I never mentioned them and Wen never mentioned them and they existed between us the way the ship existed between us: obvious, structural, and never discussed.

The bank letters had started eight months before the typhoon. I know because I was the one who took the mail when we docked—this was part of the cook's duty on a ship this small, the same way taking out garbage is part of a cook's duty in a restaurant, you are the person who interfaces with the ordinary world so that everyone else can remain in the floating one. The first letter came in a cream-colored envelope with a Hong Kong return address and the logo of a bank I recognized from advertisements in ferry terminals. I put it in the galley drawer with the rest of the mail. Wen took it. The second letter came six weeks later. Same envelope. Wen took that one too.

By the fourth letter the cream envelopes had stopped disappearing from the drawer.

By the sixth I started putting them in the drawer without mentioning them. I don't know why. It wasn't discretion, exactly. It was something more like embarrassment—the kind you feel when you've witnessed something you weren't meant to see, and the only kindness available is to pretend you're blind.

There were eleven envelopes in the galley drawer when the typhoon hit. I know because I counted them later—not on the ship, afterward, in the hospital in Guam, when they gave me my personal effects in a plastic bag and the bag contained, among other things, eleven cream-colored envelopes so waterlogged that the bank's logo had dissolved into a blue-green smear, like a bruise.

The minestrone boiled over. I cleaned the stove. The cutting boards slipped and I wedged them back. The hull made a sound that was not the sound it had been making before—a new sound, lower, more sustained, as though the ship was clearing its throat or trying to speak—and I turned the burner off and stood in the galley with my hand still on the pot and listened.

---

Morning of the second day. I think. The light through the galley porthole was greyish-white, which could have been morning or afternoon or simply the color the world had become. The storm was louder now. Not in the way you expect loudness to escalate—not a building crescendo—but in the way a headache is louder when you've had it long enough: the same volume, but it has eaten into you, claimed space, become structural. The hull was groaning.

I don't know how to describe that sound except by reaching for comparisons that belong to my life and not to the sea. It sounded like the radiator in the apartment where I grew up in Taichung, the one that would tick and moan in winter as the pipes expanded. It sounded like the creak of a wooden chair when a heavy person leans back in it—the sound of material being asked to hold more than it wants to. It sounded, worst of all, like the noise my grandmother's bed frame made in the months before she died, when she shifted in her sleep and the wood complained under a body that weighed almost nothing, as though the bed were already tired of bearing even that much.

Wen came below.

She walked into the galley with her hands held slightly out from her sides, the way you hold them when they hurt. I saw why: the skin across her palms and the base of her fingers was raw and broken—blistered from the wheel, then torn open, then blistered again over the torn places. The flesh was the deep red of something that is not yet infected but is thinking about it. She sat down at the galley table. She opened the drawer—not the one with the envelopes; the one next to it—and took out the pack of cards.

She dealt.

We played gin rummy. This was not unusual. We played gin rummy most mornings, had done so since my second week aboard, when she had found me alone in the galley between breakfast and lunch prep and sat down across from me and dealt without asking whether I played. I learned quickly that she was better than me and that she did not let me win and that the game was not social for her. It was mechanical, ritualistic, a thing she did with her hands while whatever she was thinking continued undisturbed behind her face.

She held the cards oddly that morning—pinched between her fingertips, the edges resting against the heels of her damaged palms without pressing into the blisters. She fanned them with the delicacy of someone handling something fragile, which was wrong: they were cards, not glass, and Wen was not a delicate woman. But her hands had become something she had to work around, and so she adjusted, and we played.

The ship lurched. The cards scattered off the table. Three of them landed in the inch of water that had appeared on the galley floor overnight. I picked them up. Wen picked up the rest. We sorted our hands again. The seven of hearts was damp and had begun to curl at one corner. I put it back in my hand.

At some point Wen laid down three queens and I laughed because she'd been holding them from the deal, which was shameless, and she looked at me with an expression that almost reached amusement, and I laughed again, and then she laughed—a short sound, more like a cough voluntarily extended, and it was so startling in the context of the groaning hull and the grey water beyond the porthole that we both stopped and listened to the silence that followed it, as though the laugh had broken something and we were checking to see what.

We kept playing.

Sometime later—one hand? three?—the hull made a sound I had not heard before: a deep, resonant crack, not loud but *felt*, the way you feel a bass note in your sternum, and everything in the galley that was not bolted down jumped a quarter-inch to starboard. A jar of rice fell from its shelf and shattered. The overhead light swung. The water on the floor moved like something alive.

I looked at Wen. She had heard it. I could see that she had heard it in the stillness of her face, which was the stillness of a person absorbing information they already expected, the way you absorb the news of a death you knew was coming. Her eyes dropped to her cards. She rearranged something in her hand.

She played the seven of clubs.

I picked it up because it completed a run I'd been building, and we played the hand out, and she won, and she shuffled, and she dealt another.

---

I don't know when the pumps failed. I know that the sound of them—a persistent mechanical thudding that had become so constant I'd stopped hearing it—stopped. And in the way that you only notice the ticking of a clock when it ceases, the silence where the pumps had been was enormous, a new kind of loudness, an absence that pressed against the inside of the hull like a held breath.

The water on the galley floor rose past my ankles by the time I registered what had happened.

Wen went on deck.

I followed her to the companionway. I stood at the bottom of the steps and looked up through the hatch into a world that did not look like a world—it looked like the inside of a washing machine, everything motion and white water and a wind that had a sound like sheet metal being torn. The rain was not falling. It was horizontal. It was being *thrown*.

Wen climbed up. She was carrying a coil of line she'd taken from the locker outside my galley—I knew that line; it was old braided nylon, half-inch, fraying where it had been cleated too often, and it had a dark stain at one end that might have been oil or might have been something older. I'd hung a dishrag from it once, to dry. It was that close to my daily life. It was that ordinary.

She went to the mast.

I could see her from the hatchway, or I could see parts of her—the storm edited her in and out of visibility, spray and gusts erasing her and returning her in fragments, so that I saw: her arm looping the line around the mast; her hands, the ruined ones, pulling the rope through with a motion that must have been excruciating and that she performed with the same mechanical economy she brought to dealing cards; the knots, one and then another, each one tight and workmanlike, not dramatic, not theatrical, the knots of a woman making herself fast; the rope biting into the fabric of her oilskin, compressing the canvas into the shape of her ribs.

She did not look at me. I don't think she knew I was watching, or if she knew, it was not relevant. She was doing a thing that needed to be done. The ship needed a captain. She was the captain. If the sea took her off the deck, the ship would be empty, and an empty ship is an abandoned ship, and an abandoned ship belongs to whoever claims it, and the only people who would claim the *Mara Celeste* now were the men in Bermuda with their liens and their notarized forms. She was not performing sacrifice. She was filing a counter-claim with her body.

The wind hit a register I had not heard before—lower, more sustained, a sound that belonged to industrial machinery and not to weather. I watched the spray
